Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Rubrique : Santé publique
Date du flux : 18/11/2026
Auteur : Evelyn Lepka de Lima; Ana Angélica Lindoso; Giovanna Mariah Orlandi; Suely Fukasava; Catia Martinez; Julio Croda; C Robert Horsburgh Jr; Otavio Ranzani; Meredith B Brooks; Jason R Andrews
Titre d'origine : Loss to follow-up during tuberculosis treatment and 5-year mortality in Brazil: A target trial emulation

ARTICLE :
Figures
Abstract
Background
Loss to follow-up (LTFU) during tuberculosis treatment is a major programmatic gap, but how much excess mortality it causes has been difficult to estimate, because individuals who disengage differ from those who do not, and they must survive long enough to be recorded as having disengaged. Quantifying this excess and identifying which populations are at greatest risk are critical to informing program design and resource allocation.
Methods and findings
We followed 171,048 people aged 15 years or older starting a first course of tuberculosis treatment in São Paulo State, Brazil, between 2013 and 2023, linking surveillance and mortality registries; 20,830 (12.2%) were LTFU, defined as interruption of treatment for at least 30 consecutive days. Among those LTFU, 65% had received directly observed therapy (DOT). Using a clone-censor-weight target trial emulation, we contrasted two strategies over 60 months from the first day of treatment: disengagement at any point during the first 6 months and remaining in care throughout. Analyses were adjusted for age, sex, race, education, HIV status, diabetes, alcohol use, drug use, incarceration, homelessness, hospitalization at diagnosis, clinical form of tuberculosis, DOT, and municipality. A rolling landmark analysis addressed the timing of disengagement and cause-specific mortality excess. LTFU increased standardized 5-year mortality by 2.49 percentage points (95% CI [1.94, 3.17]). In a rolling landmark analysis, tuberculosis accounted for 61% of the 5-year excess mortality. Relative effects were largest in younger, stably housed individuals, whose baseline mortality was low; the largest absolute excess fell on people living with HIV (5.16 percentage points, 95% CI [3.76, 6.60]). The excess was similar for disengagement at any point in the first 4 months of treatment and attenuated thereafter. Limitations include the absence from the registry of severity markers such as radiographic extent and bacillary load, so residual confounding cannot be excluded.
Conclusions
Despite high DOT coverage, disengagement during the first 6 months of tuberculosis treatment was common and increased 5-year mortality under the stated identification assumptions, with the excess concentrated in deaths attributed to tuberculosis. Interventions that provide support throughout treatment should be tested for their effectiveness in sustaining engagement and reducing mortality.
Author summary
Why was this study done?
- People who interrupt tuberculosis treatment have a higher risk of death, but it remains unclear how much of this risk is attributable to treatment interruption itself.
- Estimating this impact is challenging because people who interrupt treatment differ from those who remain in care, and the way these groups are compared can lead to misleading results.
- Understanding how treatment interruption affects deaths from tuberculosis and other causes, including years after treatment begins, is important for improving tuberculosis care.
What did the researchers do and find?
- We studied 171,048 people starting tuberculosis treatment in São Paulo State, Brazil, between 2013 and 2023, using health records to examine mortality over 5 years.
- We estimated that interrupting treatment increased the 5-year risk of death by ~25 additional deaths per 1,000 people, with tuberculosis itself the leading cause of these additional deaths.
- The increase in mortality was similar when treatment was interrupted during any of the first 4 months after starting treatment, and people living with HIV experienced the largest absolute increase in risk.
What do these findings mean?
- Interrupting tuberculosis treatment may contribute to deaths occurring years after treatment begins, making sustained engagement in care important for long-term survival.
- Although most people who interrupted treatment had received directly observed therapy, our findings suggest that tuberculosis programs need approaches that go beyond observing medication intake to help patients complete treatment.
- Because the study used routinely collected health records, we could not fully account for differences in disease severity or changes in patients’ health during treatment, and some patients were excluded because of incomplete records or transfers.

Introduction
Tuberculosis remains a major cause of infectious disease mortality globally, accounting for an estimated 1.23 million deaths in 2024 [1]. Achieving progress in reducing this burden depends critically on maintaining high rates of completion of curative therapy. Despite the availability of effective drug regimens for decades, many high-burden countries have struggled to translate the high cure rates observed in clinical trials and controlled settings into everyday practice [2]. Mortality trends in WHO Region of the Americas further highlight this challenge, with limited progress overall and increasing mortality in several countries, including Brazil, since 2015 [1].
Loss to follow-up (LTFU) over the standard 6 months of tuberculosis treatment represents an important programmatic gap in tuberculosis care and a major contributor to adverse outcomes. When LTFU occurs, consequences include Mycobacterium tuberculosis drug resistance, ongoing transmission, and increased mortality [1]. However, quantifying these effects presents several challenges. LTFU is not a random event, and a range of demographic and clinical characteristics have been associated with increased risk, including male sex, younger age, lower educational attainment, HIV co-infection, prior tuberculosis, and substance use [1,2].
Estimating the impact of LTFU on mortality is therefore complicated by confounding, as factors influencing disengagement from care also affect subsequent outcomes [3]. These effects can act in multiple directions: individuals with greater social vulnerabilities may be more likely to interrupt treatment and have poor outcomes, while individuals with more severe disease, who are at greatest risk of death, might be less likely to discontinue therapy than those with less advanced disease and few symptoms.
Comparisons between individuals who interrupt treatment and those who complete it are also subject to several distinct forms of immortal-time bias [4]. When exposure is assigned at treatment initiation according to how treatment later ended, individuals are classified as LTFU on the basis of an event that occurs only after part of their treatment has been survived: anyone who dies before disengaging is recorded as an on-treatment death and can only appear in the comparison group. The time from treatment initiation to disengagement, which may occur at any point during treatment, is therefore immortal-time for the LTFU group, and counting it as exposed biases the comparison toward a protective effect of LTFU [5]. Furthermore, because programmatic LTFU is declared only after a specified period of absence, incorrectly attributing that interval to the LTFU group can introduce additional immortal-time bias. Conversely, defining the comparator as individuals who complete therapy introduces immortal-time bias from the other direction, since treatment completion is itself a post-baseline outcome attainable only by surviving to the end of treatment.
Prior studies have consistently found higher mortality after LTFU [6–11], but most compared individuals lost to follow-up with those recorded as cured or as having completed treatment [6,7,9,11], a group that necessarily survived to treatment completion, thereby conditioning the comparison on survival. None has systematically addressed the immortal-time biases described above, so the magnitude of the excess mortality caused by disengagement remains unknown. Quantifying the effects of LTFU on mortality and identifying the groups at greatest risk of harm from LTFU are both important for prioritizing resources and developing effective strategies to address this problem.
We therefore aimed to address these methodological challenges and estimate the effect of LTFU on mortality, under explicitly stated identification assumptions, using a large population-based cohort linking tuberculosis surveillance and mortality data over long-term follow-up. We set out to answer three questions: how much excess mortality is attributable to disengagement; whether that effect depends on when during therapy disengagement occurs; and in which populations the absolute excess is largest. We additionally examined the causes of death underlying the excess to assess whether it is consistent with a causal pathway through interrupted therapy.
Methods
Study design and data sources
We conducted a retrospective cohort study using data from TBweb, the electronic tuberculosis surveillance system of the São Paulo State Tuberculosis Program, and the Brazilian Mortality Information System (SIM). TBweb is an electronic surveillance platform used to notify and monitor all individuals diagnosed with tuberculosis in São Paulo State. The system is integrated with the national Notifiable Diseases Information System (SINAN), and uses the SINAN identification number as a unique person-level identifier, enabling longitudinal follow-up and linkage of multiple tuberculosis episodes for the same individual. SIM is Brazil’s national mortality registry, which records all deaths nationwide. Death certificates follow the international format, and the underlying cause of death is assigned by trained coders based on the reported sequence of conditions. The quality of SIM has recently been evaluated: registration completeness has improved over time and the proportion of deaths assigned an ill-defined or otherwise uninformative underlying cause fell substantially between 2000 and 2015, with the remaining shortfalls concentrated in the North and Northeast rather than in São Paulo State [12,13]. The study extract included the underlying cause of death; the contributing conditions recorded on the remaining lines of the certificate were available from the same linkage and were used in a secondary analysis. TBweb and SIM records were probabilistically linked to identify deaths during follow-up (Section B in S1 Appendix). The study included all tuberculosis notifications recorded in TBweb between January 1, 2013, and December 31, 2023, with administrative censoring on December 31, 2024 to allow at least 1-year of follow-up. Data extraction and linkage were performed in January 2025. No prospective protocol or statistical analysis plan was published or registered; the analyses that were planned, and the changes made during the study and in response to peer review, are described under Changes to the analysis. This study is reported as per the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guideline (S1 Checklist) and, for the target trial emulation, as per the TrAnsparent ReportinG of studies Emulating a Target trial (TARGET) guideline (S2 Checklist); the specification and emulation of the target trial protocol are reported in Table E in S1 Appendix.
Study population
The study cohort included individuals aged 15 years or older at the time of their first new tuberculosis notification in São Paulo State, Brazil, between 2013 and 2023. Each individual contributed a single episode: their earliest new-case notification, excluding notifications later reclassified as not tuberculosis or lacking a recorded treatment outcome. Whether that episode ended in LTFU defined the exposure. We excluded individuals with missing or implausible dates (e.g., death occurring before treatment initiation date), administrative transfers outside São Paulo State or Brazil, or no recorded treatment start date. Later notifications did not contribute to exposure, but were used to ascertain cause of death. All counts refer to individuals, not notifications.
Exposures and outcomes
LTFU during the first tuberculosis episode was the exposure of interest. Under Brazilian national guidelines, LTFU is defined as treatment interruption for at least 30 consecutive days [14]. Therefore, the date recorded in the registry is the LTFU declaration date: the first day on which LTFU can be classified, after the individual has gone at least 30 days without documented medication use. To approximate the date on which treatment was actually interrupted, we defined the interruption date as 30 days before the declaration date. Where each date enters the analysis differs between the two designs and is specified below.
Death was ascertained using two data sources. First, deaths were identified within TBweb based on-treatment outcomes recorded. Second, deaths were identified through probabilistic linkage with SIM, as described in section B in S1 Appendix. When date-of-death discrepancies between sources were identified, records were verified for individual identity and administrative consistency, and the earliest recorded date of death was used. Outcomes were classified as tuberculosis-attributable deaths and nontuberculosis deaths. Tuberculosis-attributable deaths were defined using ICD-10 codes for underlying causes from SIM, supplemented by TBweb case-closure classifications. SIM records an underlying cause, defined as the condition that initiated the sequence of events leading to death, together with the contributing conditions entered on the remaining certificate lines. Deaths were counted as tuberculosis-attributable only where tuberculosis was the underlying cause; we repeated the cause attribution counting tuberculosis recorded on any line as a secondary analysis (Section C.4 in S1 Appendix). Nontuberculosis deaths were defined as all other causes.
Covariates for all models were age group, sex, race, education, HIV status, diabetes, alcohol use, drug use, incarceration, homelessness, hospitalization at diagnosis, clinical tuberculosis classification, directly observed therapy (DOT), and municipality of treatment classified according to the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) rural–urban typology [15], custody settings being folded into the urban reference level because that category is collinear with incarceration. All were defined at the time of treatment initiation, as TBweb records these characteristics at notification and does not reliably update them during treatment. Hospitalization at diagnosis is not routine in Brazil: the main indications are clinical severity, management of comorbidity including advanced HIV disease, and social circumstances in which outpatient treatment is not feasible. DOT is the practice of a person watching the patient take their tuberculosis medication in real time, and forms part of the broader strategy promoted by the World Health Organization to support adherence to treatment. DOT is recommended for everyone treated for tuberculosis in Brazil but is not always achievable, for example where an individual lives far from the treating facility, where work schedules conflict with daily observation, or where housing is unstable.
Statistical analysis
Multiple imputation.
Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations with random-forest predictors, assuming the data were missing at random [16]. The imputation model included all baseline covariates, the exposure, event indicators, and follow-up times, along with three predictors of missingness not in the adjustment set: calendar year of treatment start, recorded mental health condition, and setting of diagnosis. Missingness was related to recorded characteristics, most strongly to calendar year of treatment start and, for education, to social circumstances. The imputation model therefore conditioned on these, along with the complete outcome and follow-up time (Section D.1 in S1 Appendix). Imputation was applied to covariates only. We generated five imputed datasets. Multivariable analyses were fitted separately in each imputed dataset and pooled using Rubin’s rules. Complete-case analyses were conducted as sensitivity analyses (Section D.2 in in S1 Appendix).
Causal analyses: Target trial emulation and rolling landmark
The primary analysis emulated a target trial from the start of treatment [17,18], contrasting two strategies: disengagement from treatment at any point during the first six months, and remaining engaged throughout that window. Because an individual’s future disengagement cannot be known at treatment start, each individual was cloned into both strategies. Each clone was censored at the point at which the observed history diverged from its assigned strategy (for the continued engagement strategy, the recorded LTFU declaration date) and the resulting informative censoring was corrected with inverse-probability-of-censoring weights [19] estimated from the covariates listed above together with a municipality random intercept. An individual who was alive and still engaged within the window was compatible with both strategies, so deaths occurring at that time point contributed to both arms; surviving to the point of disengagement was not a condition of entering the analysis. Standardized cumulative mortality risk was computed under each strategy and contrasted at 60 months as a risk difference and a risk ratio. Follow-up was not extended beyond 60 months because the proportion of the cohort with sufficient follow-up declines steeply thereafter. Confidence intervals were obtained from a bootstrap that resamples municipalities, to allow for nonindependence of individuals treated in the same municipality; because São Paulo city contributes one third of the cohort, it was included in every replicate with its individuals resampled, and the remaining 639 municipalities were resampled as whole clusters (Section I in in S1 Appendix).
The timing of disengagement was addressed with a separate rolling landmark design [20]. One landmark trial was opened for each day on which any individual was declared LTFU: individuals declared on that day formed the exposed arm, individuals still in care on that day formed the comparator, and follow-up for both arms began on that day. The 30-day grace period required by the LTFU definition therefore applies symmetrically, since both arms must be alive and event-free at the landmark. Trials were stacked and fitted with a single Cox model adjusted for the covariates listed above and a municipality random intercept, and absolute risks were obtained by g-formula standardization [21] to the disengaging population. Confidence intervals for the landmark risk differences were obtained with the same municipality-resampling bootstrap as the target trial emulation, rebuilding the stacked trials in each replicate; hazard ratios reported in sensitivity analyses use standard errors clustered on individual, because individuals contribute to more than one trial (Section I in S1 Appendix). Because the proportional-hazards assumption was rejected over a five-year horizon, the exposure was given a separate coefficient in each of five disjoint follow-up periods and the cumulative hazard assembled piecewise, so that the standardized risks do not assume a constant hazard ratio.
The two designs use different time origins (treatment start for the target trial emulation, the individual’s own declaration date for the landmark) and their magnitudes are therefore not comparable. The landmark exposed arm is smaller than the cohort total lost to follow-up because exposure must be indexed on a day of disengagement within the treatment course (Section A in S1 Appendix). Both were repeated within subgroups defined by age group, sex, HIV status, homelessness, drug resistance, and calendar period of treatment initiation. The two designs, and the time origin each uses, are shown in Fig 1. Both designs identify a causal effect only under assumptions the data cannot verify: that the arms are exchangeable conditional on the measured baseline covariates, so that no unmeasured determinant of both disengagement and death remains; that censoring at divergence from an assigned strategy is uninformative given those covariates and the weight model; and that both strategies were possible for every individual at the time origin. Unmeasured severity is the assumption most likely to fail, and Section F in S1 Appendix quantifies how strong such a confounder would need to be to explain the estimate away.

Cause-specific analyses
To assess whether the association between LTFU and mortality is consistent with the effects of treatment interruption or reflects residual confounding, we repeated the rolling landmark cohort analysis using cause-specific mortality outcomes, evaluating deaths due to tuberculosis and other causes. We utilized this design as the question concerns deaths after LTFU, whereas the target trial emulation shares deaths occurring before the two strategies diverge and dilutes the cause-specific contrast. Cause-specific Cox models were fitted by censoring deaths from the alternate cause at the time of occurrence. Cumulative incidence functions were then constructed (Aalen–Johansen) so that the tuberculosis and nontuberculosis components sum to the all-cause risk difference. Deaths whose cause could not be classified were included in the nontuberculosis class.
Sensitivity analyses
We conducted sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the primary findings. First, cause-specific analyses were restricted to deaths with an ICD-10 classification from SIM only (Section C.2 in S1 Appendix), and were repeated counting tuberculosis recorded on any line of the death certificate rather than only as the underlying cause (Section C.4 in in S1 Appendix). Second, analyses were stratified by calendar period (Section E in S1 Appendix). Third, we repeated the primary rolling landmark cohort analysis in the complete-case set, restricted to individuals with complete data for all covariates (Section D.2 in S1 Appendix). Fourth, we quantified sensitivity to unmeasured confounding by computing an E-value for the primary risk ratio, which gives the minimum strength of association an unmeasured confounder would need with both disengagement and mortality to explain the estimate away (Section F in S1 Appendix). Fifth, we repeated the primary analysis without the municipality random intercept, and with confidence intervals obtained by resampling individuals or by resampling all municipalities as clusters (Section I in S1 Appendix). In addition, we conducted descriptive supplementary analyses of temporal trends in LTFU incidence and post-LTFU outcomes across the study period. Finally, to evaluate how much of the variation in published estimates reflects study design rather than the underlying association, we applied the design used by most prior studies to this cohort, with follow-up from treatment initiation and a comparator of individuals recorded as cured, holding the covariates and horizon fixed. Because prior studies report relative measures, that comparison is made on the hazard ratio scale.
Changes to the analysis
The study questions, cohort definition, and exposure and outcome definitions were established before analysis. Several analytical decisions were made during the study rather than pre-specified. The 60-month follow-up horizon was selected based on the availability of follow-up data, and a period-flexible model was adopted after the proportional-hazards assumption was rejected.
The analytical approach was also refined in response to peer review. The original fixed-month landmark analysis was replaced with a rolling landmark design anchored at each individual’s LTFU declaration date to address immortal-time bias, and the target trial emulation became the primary analysis. We also added a municipality random intercept to the censoring model of the target trial emulation to address geographic clustering.
Software and reproducibility
Cohort construction and data management were performed in Python 3.13, and statistical analyses were conducted in R 4.5. Code and a reproducible analysis pipeline are available at https://github.com/evelepka/ltfu-outcomes-causal-inference and archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23539289. The minimal de-identified dataset underlying these analyses is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24115952.
Ethics
Written permission for secondary use of surveillance data was obtained from the São Paulo State Health Department, and the study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Instituto de Infectologia Emílio Ribas, São Paulo, Brazil (Plataforma Brasil ethics registration CAAE 98567826.0.0000.0061; approval 8.512.623, 16 June 2026; amendment 8.639.422, 10 August 2026).

Results
Study population
TBweb recorded 235,629 individuals with tuberculosis between 2013 and 2023, of whom 219,282 had a first tuberculosis episode. Of these, 6,552 were excluded due to a change of diagnosis, 12,460 due to missing or incomplete outcome information, and 1,861 due to transfer during treatment to another state or country. Further exclusions included individuals aged <15 years (n = 6,178) and deaths recorded on or before treatment initiation (n = 549). Episodes with recorded outcome dates outside the study period (2013–2023) were also excluded (n = 17,834), and 21 individuals whose tuberculosis was identified only post-mortem were excluded as never at risk for LTFU. Finally, 2,779 cases with missing or inconsistent treatment dates (800 LTFU, 1,979 continued-in-care) were excluded from the primary analysis to ensure consistent time-on-treatment alignment. The final primary cohort comprised 171,048 individuals (Fig 2), 97.2% of the 175,998 adults with a first tuberculosis episode ending within the study period. Of these, 20,830 (12.2%) experienced LTFU during their first episode. Among individuals who were not LTFU, 135,699 (90.3%) were programmatically classified as cured, 12,336 (8.2%) as deaths (5,520 tuberculosis-related and 6,816 nontuberculosis-related), 1,044 (0.7%) as treatment failure, and 1,139 (0.8%) as other outcomes, including regimen changes due to toxicity.
Flow of individuals from all tuberculosis notifications recorded in TBweb between 2013 and 2023 to the analytic cohort of 171,048, with the number excluded at each step and the reason for exclusion.
Compared with individuals who continued in care, those who were LTFU were younger (median age 33 years, interquartile range [IQR] 25–42, versus 37, IQR 27–51), more frequently male (78.7% versus 70.4%), and reported higher prevalence of homelessness (10.6% versus 2.3%), alcohol use (29.9% versus 16.2%), drug use (35.6% versus 13.9%), and HIV (11.4% versus 7.6%). They were also more often hospitalized at diagnosis (32.9% versus 23.6%) and less likely to receive DOT (65.4% versus 74.4%). (Table 1)
Annual LTFU risk rose from approximately 10% in 2013–2018 to ~15% in 2021–2022, coinciding with the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. Drug-susceptibility testing (DST) yielded a conclusive result in 21.7% of the cohort (n = 37,190/171,048). Among those tested, 1.51% (n = 562) had rifampin-resistant or multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and 2.25% (n = 836) had isoniazid mono-resistant disease. LTFU rates were broadly similar across drug resistance categories: 11.7% (95% CI [9.3, 14.7]) among individuals with rifampin- or multidrug-resistant TB, 13.5% (95% CI [13.1, 13.9]) in the drug-sensitive group, and 11.8% (95% CI [11.7, 12.0]) among those without a recorded DST result. LTFU was declared at a median of 3.88 months (IQR [2.11, 5.43]) from treatment start, and at a median of 3.12 months among the 17,150 declared within the first six months (Fig 3A).

Mortality after LTFU
Among the 20,830 individuals who experienced LTFU, 9,395 (45.1%) subsequently began a retreatment episode, 453 (2.2%) died without returning to treatment, and 10,982 (52.7%) had no further recorded episode (Fig 3D). Among those who returned, 4,010 (42.7%) were cured, and 4,307 (45.8%) were again LTFU. Post-LTFU observation totaled 111,703 person-years, with a median of 5.0 years (IQR [2.5, 8.0]) per individual; 1,668 (8.0%) died, at a median of 17.5 months (IQR [6.7, 38.9]) after LTFU, a crude mortality rate of 14.9 deaths per 1,000 person-years (95% CI [14.2, 15.7]).
Crude five-year mortality after LTFU varied more than 5-fold across baseline characteristics (Fig 4): 20.0% among people living with HIV (PLHIV) compared with 6.3% among HIV–negative individuals; 17.5% among individuals hospitalized at diagnosis versus 3.0% among those who were not; 14.5% among individuals experiencing homelessness compared with 7.1% among housed individuals; 11.0% among those reporting alcohol use versus 6.6% among those not; and rising with age from 4.4% at 15–24 years to 16.4% at 65 years or above. Mortality was highest among individuals disengaging earliest, falling from 12.3% among those who disengaged in the first month of therapy to 4.1% in the sixth.

Effect of LTFU on mortality
The primary analysis emulated a target trial from the start of treatment, contrasting disengagement at any point during the first 6 months with continued engagement. At 60 months, standardized mortality risk was 11.79% under the disengagement strategy against 9.30% under continued engagement, an absolute risk difference of 2.49 percentage points (95% CI [1.94, 3.17]) and a risk ratio of 1.27 (95% CI [1.24, 1.31]) (Fig 5).

Cause-specific evidence: TB-attributable versus non-TB mortality
A cause of death was available from either source for 86.4% of deaths within 5 years in the exposed arm and 88.1% in the comparator arm. A cause coded in the national mortality registry was available for 37.2% and 41.9%, respectively; the remainder was taken from the programmatic outcome recorded in TBweb. When both sources cited the same cause of death (n = 2,618), they agreed on tuberculosis versus nontuberculosis attribution in 76.2% of cases (Cohen's κ = 0.52).
The excess was concentrated in deaths attributed to tuberculosis. On the absolute scale, the 5-year excess of 2.68 percentage points (95% CI [2.28, 3.24]) was partitioned into 1.64 percentage points attributed to tuberculosis (95% CI [1.28, 1.93]) and 1.04 percentage points not attributed to tuberculosis (95% CI [0.80, 1.49]). Tuberculosis therefore accounted for 61% of the total excess. Restricting cause of death to ICD-10 codes recorded in the mortality registry gave the same ordering (Section C.2 in S1 Appendix). Counting tuberculosis recorded on any line of the death certificate rather than only as the underlying cause classified 26% more deaths as tuberculosis-related and raised the tuberculosis share of the excess from 61% to 63% (1.68 versus 1.64 percentage points), with the reclassified deaths falling in both arms (Section C.4 in S1 Appendix).
Effect modification of LTFU
Effects were compared across subgroups within the same target trial emulation, at 60 months (Fig 6A and 6B). On the relative scale, the risk ratio was highest in the youngest individuals (15–24 years, 1.90, 95% CI [1.67, 2.16]) and declined with age, to 1.42 (95% CI [1.37, 1.52]) at 25–44 years, 1.23 (95% CI [1.16, 1.30]) at 45–64 years, and 1.07 (95% CI [0.99, 1.15]) at 65 years or above. PLHIV had a lower risk ratio (1.20, 95% CI [1.14, 1.25]) than HIV–negative individuals (1.27, 95% CI [1.23, 1.33]), and individuals experiencing homelessness had a lower ratio (1.09, 95% CI [1.01, 1.17]) than housed persons (1.27, 95% CI [1.24, 1.32]). Estimates were similar by sex (female 1.28, 95% CI [1.20, 1.39]; male 1.25, 95% CI [1.21, 1.30]) and across calendar periods (2013–2019: 1.28, 95% CI [1.23, 1.33]; 2020–2023: 1.26, 95% CI [1.19, 1.36]).
On the absolute scale the ordering reverses. The 60-month risk difference was largest among PLHIV (5.16 percentage points, 95% CI [3.76, 6.60]), more than twice the figure in HIV–negative persons (2.16, 95% CI [1.65, 2.84]), and rose with age from 1.96 (95% CI [1.52, 2.77]) at 15–24 years to 3.34 (95% CI [2.27, 4.46]) at 45–64 years. Among individuals experiencing homelessness it was 1.87 percentage points (95% CI [0.14, 3.47]), and among the small group with drug-resistant tuberculosis, 8.77 percentage points (95% CI [1.46, 14.52]).
Discussion
LTFU during tuberculosis treatment raised standardized 5-year mortality by 2.49 percentage points, and the excess was concentrated in tuberculosis-attributable deaths. 5-year risk differences were similar for disengagement at any point during the first 4 months of treatment, attenuating thereafter. The relative effects of LTFU were largest among younger, stably housed individuals, in whom the competing-mortality baseline is low, whereas on the absolute scale the greatest LTFU-attributable mortality burden fell on PLHIV. These findings, in a setting with high DOT coverage, point to the need for more effective models of care engagement throughout the course of treatment, particularly among PLHIV.
